Two Races, One Scoreboard

America is winning the race to build the smartest machine. China is winning the race to put a good enough one in everything. Asking which country is ahead only makes sense once you say which race you mean.

By Josh Pilcher · Monday, November 9, 2026
Scroll

The expensive race, indoors

The lead lives in rooms like this.

Capital, chips and electricity, converted into computing power. Keep scrolling. The other side stopped trying to win this room, and started giving the results away.

Photograph via IBM. Rows like these are where the American lead actually lives. The question I keep coming back to is what happens when the other side stops trying to win this room and starts giving the results away.

I wrote this on Monday evening, Central, working from sources dated through November 9, 2026. If I could not tie a number to a source I trusted, I left it out.

The Bottom Line

There is no single AI race, so there is no single winner. America owns the expensive frontier: the best models, the chips they train on and the money that pays for both.

China owns the cheap layer underneath: open models anyone can download, priced so low they are close to free, spreading through the world's software faster than American models are.

Each side is short on a different thing. America is short on electricity and on time, because its lead is financed with borrowed money that has to be repaid by revenue that has not arrived yet.

China is short on memory chips and on the machines that print advanced silicon, and no amount of clever software fully makes up for either. Neither side has turned its strength into a lock on the other.

So the honest answer to who is winning is a question back: winning what? The winner of the whole contest will be whichever country fixes its own bottleneck first. Everything below is the evidence I would put behind that sentence.

Chapter One

The Rulers

Before arguing about the gap, you have to ask who is holding the ruler. The gap changes size depending on which test you pick, and that fact alone explains half the shouting.

Start with the simplest version of the story, because it is mostly true. The best AI models in the world are American.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, the most cited independent scoreboard of model quality, the top of the table in late October 2026 was Gemini 4 Carbon at 59 points, Claude Opus 5.5 at 58 and GPT-6 Astra at 57.

The best Chinese entry, Kimi K3.1 Pro, scored 46. Thirteen points at the top of that table is a real gap.

It is the distance between a model that handles long, tangled professional work reliably and one that handles most of it, most of the time.

Now pick a different ruler and watch the gap shrink. On LiveBench, a benchmark built to resist cheating by rotating in fresh questions, DeepSeek's best model scored 81.1 in October against 83.4 for Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1.

That is a difference of about 3 percent, inside the range where the choice of test matters as much as the choice of model.

On Stanford's Arena leaderboard, which ranks models by how human voters rate their answers in blind comparisons, the gap was 2.7 percent in March, and the lead had already changed hands several times since early 2025.

And on one slice of LiveBench, agentic coding, where a model works through a programming task on its own, DeepSeek actually led, 77.3 to 66.1.

Then pick the ruler the United States government uses, and the gap opens up again.

NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation tested DeepSeek's V4 Pro in May 2026 on nine tests it had committed to in advance, including tests the labs could not rehearse for. Its verdict: about eight months behind the frontier.

On a held-out software engineering test, the Chinese model solved 44 percent of problems against 78 percent for the American frontier. On a semi-private reasoning test, 46 percent against 79 percent.

The pattern across all four rulers is consistent once you see it. On public tests, where everyone can practice, China looks close.

On private tests, where nobody can, the American lead is wide. The gap is partly a property of the models.

It is also partly a property of the exam.

There is one more split inside the numbers, and it matters for everything that follows. The 46 scored by Kimi K3.1 Pro belongs to a model whose weights, the actual file you can download and run yourself, only shipped on November 4.

The best Chinese models you could actually download and run at the end of October scored 32. That is a 26 point gap between America's frontier and China's best freely available model, far wider than any headline about parity suggests.

China's closed frontier is close-ish.

China's open frontier, the part the rest of the world can build on, is much further back on the hardest tests, and much cheaper, and improving on a schedule set by Beijing's labs rather than by Washington's export rules.

Hold both halves of that sentence. Everything I argue from here lives in the tension between them.

Same models. Four rulers. Gaps of 3 percent, 13 points, 26 points and 8 months. Anyone who gives you one number is selling something.

Chapter Two

The Chokepoints

Models are software. Software runs on chips, chips run on memory, and memory is where China's race actually gets decided.

If the benchmark gap is an argument, the hardware gap is a census. Epoch AI, which counts AI computing hardware the way demographers count people, estimates that Huawei will produce about 880,000 H100-equivalents of AI compute in 2026.

An H100-equivalent is the standard yardstick: the computing power of one Nvidia H100, the chip that trained most of the current generation of models. Nvidia will produce about 23 million.

Huawei's entire national champion, working flat out, makes less than 4 percent of what one American company makes. That is not a gap you close with a good quarter.

It is a difference in industrial scale.

Look one level deeper and the picture sharpens, because China's binding constraint is not the processor. It is memory.

Modern AI chips are useless without HBM, high bandwidth memory, the stacked memory packages that feed data to the processor fast enough to keep it busy.

The HBM market belongs to three companies, none of them Chinese: SK Hynix of South Korea holds about half, Samsung a third, Micron of Idaho most of the rest.

China's own memory maker, CXMT, produces its newest HBM at yields of 20 to 30 percent, against roughly 70 percent at SK Hynix. Yield is the share of chips that come off the line working.

At 25 percent yield you are not manufacturing memory, you are manufacturing scrap with occasional memory in it.

Epoch estimates domestic HBM can equip only about 16 percent of Huawei's chip output, which means most of those 880,000 processors are waiting on memory that has to come from somewhere else.

Huawei knew this was coming and stockpiled more than 10 million HBM stacks while it still could. The reserve runs out in 2026.

Underneath memory sits the deepest chokepoint of all: the machines that make the machines.

Every leading AI chip on earth is printed by TSMC in Taiwan, using lithography machines from ASML in the Netherlands, which holds 100 percent of the market for the EUV machines that print the finest features.

China has never received a single EUV machine.

Its champion, SMIC, prints near-7-nanometer chips using older DUV machines pushed through multiple exposures, a slower and more expensive way to reach a similar result, the industrial equivalent of writing a letter four times to get darker ink.

And even TSMC's output has a queue: its advanced packaging capacity, the CoWoS process that binds processors to memory, is sold out through 2026 with lead times of a year or more.

The whole world's frontier runs through two companies and one island. That fact constrains Washington's plans almost as much as Beijing's.

Against that wall, Washington built a fence, and the history of the fence is a history of leaks. Export controls began in earnest in October 2022, when the A100 and H100 were barred from China.

They were tightened in October 2023 when Nvidia's workaround chips were caught, widened in December 2024 to cover memory and equipment, and partially reversed in January 2026, when H200 chips were cleared for sale case by case, capped at half of what Nvidia sells at home and carrying a 25 percent duty.

Each tightening worked on paper. Each one also leaked.

The Center for a New American Security put the median estimate of smuggled high-end chips at about 140,000 in 2024 alone. Epoch puts the cumulative diverted total somewhere between 290,000 and 1.6 million H100-equivalents through the end of 2025.

In March 2026, federal prosecutors in New York alleged that about $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia servers had been routed to China.

The Institute for Progress calculated that a total, airtight ban would leave America with 21 to 49 times China's newly produced compute. Airtight is doing all the work in that sentence.

With exports, smuggling and rented offshore capacity counted, Chinese-accessible compute is on track to roughly double by the end of 2027, to about 8.8 million H100-equivalents, and roughly 65 percent of it rides on American-designed chips.

The strangest exhibit in the whole fence story is sitting in Hong Kong. About 600,000 H200 chips, cleared in principle by Washington, were stockpiled there by early November 2026, waiting for Beijing to say yes.

Beijing, so far, has said no. In May 2026 it barred major Chinese firms from buying Nvidia chips at all, and Nvidia has effectively written off the market, telling investors to assume zero data center revenue from China.

So the current state of play is a reversal nobody predicted in 2022: Washington is willing to sell, Beijing is refusing to buy, and the chips sit in a warehouse while both governments claim the other is the obstacle.

Read it as strategy and it makes sense. Every H200 China refuses is demand handed to Huawei, and every year of refusal is another year of forced practice for the domestic industry China actually wants to own.

The fence taught China to climb. Now China is declining the ladder, on the theory that climbing is the point.

My conclusion from those numbers is that the production gap is structural, and it will not close this decade on current trajectories.

The usable gap is smaller, it leaks, and it leaks mostly from the American side, through legal sales, gray channels and cloud rentals. Controls bought time.

What did America do with that time? It spent.

The chokepoint, up close

20 to 30%

Chapter Three

The Money

America's lead is real. So is the bill. The frontier is being built with borrowed money, and the lenders have started pricing that fact.

The scale of American spending is difficult to say out loud without it sounding like a typo.

The four big hyperscalers, Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, spent $201.9 billion in cash on capital projects in the third quarter of 2026 alone, up 108 percent from a year earlier.

Their combined guidance for 2026 runs to roughly $720 to $740 billion, and the consensus for 2027 is about $1.04 trillion. For calibration: a trillion dollars is roughly what the United States spends on its entire military.

The AI build-out is now a second defense budget, raised privately, aimed at data centers.

The catch is where the money comes from. These companies used to fund expansion from profit.

Their combined free cash flow was $199 billion in 2025. By the first half of 2026 it had fallen to an annualized pace of about $30 billion.

Alphabet's free cash flow went negative in the third quarter. So did Meta's.

The difference is being borrowed: about a third of 2026 capital spending is debt-funded, heading for a peak near 35 percent in 2027. The credit market has noticed.

The cost of insuring Oracle's debt against default has more than doubled this year. CoreWeave, a data center company built entirely on the AI boom, pays junk-bond prices to borrow.

The IMF counted 14 large AI financing deals since 2023 tying about $300 billion of equity and $650 billion of debt to about $1.4 trillion in future revenue commitments, and used the phrase every financial historian dreads: wrong-way risk, the kind where the collateral and the borrower fail at the same time.

More than half of all investment into AI firms between 2021 and 2025 came from other AI firms. Nvidia invests in OpenAI, OpenAI commits to buy Nvidia chips, Microsoft funds the cloud, the cloud buys the chips.

You can call it an ecosystem. An accountant would call it a circle.

Anthropic's public filings, made ahead of its stock listing, show the shape of the bet in one company. Revenue in the first half of 2026 was $16.3 billion, growing fast, with its first profitable quarter in the second quarter.

Committed future spending: about $895 billion, roughly 80 percent of it non-cancelable, about $447 billion due before the end of 2030.

OpenAI's audited 2025 numbers, leaked in June, show $13.1 billion of revenue against $34 billion of costs, and about $720 billion in disclosed compute contracts. Its run rate reached just under $50 billion by September 2026 on a net basis.

These are genuinely enormous revenues, growing at speeds with few precedents in business history. They are also, today, a fraction of what has already been promised.

The American strategy, stated plainly, is to spend the money first and grow into it. It works if the growth continues.

The whole structure is a wager that it does.

China's money problem is the opposite shape.

Stanford's AI Index counted $285.9 billion of private AI investment in the United States in 2025 against $12.4 billion in China, a ratio of 23 to 1, with Stanford itself warning that its China figure understates the true total because so much Chinese spending runs through the state.

Rhodium Group estimates Chinese AI capital spending at about $139 billion in 2026, perhaps 15 to 20 percent of the American figure.

China's champions are spending from a weakening base: Alibaba, Tencent and Baidu together swung from 170 billion yuan of positive free cash flow in 2025 to negative 16 billion yuan in the first half of 2026, because they are building too.

And they are building into a price war. China has more than 1,100 large language models, most of them competing on price, and Bloomberg Intelligence forecasts the industry there may not turn profitable before 2030, though JPMorgan puts it closer to 2028.

MiniMax and Z.ai, two of the brightest Chinese labs, lost $150 billion of combined market value from their highs by late October.

Here is what I take from that: both countries are spending money they do not currently have on capacity they cannot currently fill. The difference is the failure mode.

America's is financial: if revenue growth slows before the commitments come due, the pain arrives as a credit event, suddenly and everywhere at once.

China's is industrial: if the price war runs to 2030, the pain arrives as a slow thinning of the field, lab by lab. A crash and an erosion are both survivable.

They are not the same risk, and they do not arrive on the same schedule.

Chapter Four

The Giveaway

China's answer to being locked out of the frontier was to stop guarding its own work. It gave the models away, and the world took them.

The moment the strategy became visible was January 20, 2025, when a Chinese lab called DeepSeek released a model named R1 under terms that let anyone download it, run it and build a business on it.

R1 matched the best American models of its day on math and reasoning tests. Its predecessor had been trained, in its final run, for about $5.6 million of computing time, a rounding error next to American training budgets.

A week later Nvidia lost 17 percent of its value in a single day, about $589 billion, the largest one-day loss any company had ever recorded. Investors were not really repricing Nvidia.

They were repricing the assumption that intelligence this good had to be expensive.

What followed was a flood with a deliberate shape. DeepSeek's V4, released in April 2026, is a genuinely open model under the MIT license, the most permissive terms in software.

Alibaba's Qwen family and Moonshot's Kimi models are open in a narrower sense, released under custom licenses that start charging once a business built on them passes a revenue threshold, $50 million for Qwen's flagship, $20 million for Kimi's.

That distinction matters, and I will not blur it: DeepSeek is the true giveaway, the others are free samples with a meter attached.

But from the perspective of a developer in Jakarta or Lagos or São Paulo choosing what to build on, the practical offer is the same. Chinese models, good ones, at prices roughly twelve times lower than the American equivalents.

The adoption numbers say the offer is being accepted. Chinese models took 41 percent of downloads on Hugging Face, the main library where developers get open models, in the year to February 2026, ahead of American models at 36.5 percent.

On OpenRouter, a marketplace where developers buy access to many models through one pipe, Chinese models carried about 61 percent of all tokens by May 2026, and in one week in September they carried 62 trillion tokens against 14 trillion for American models, their twenty-second straight week in front.

A token is roughly a word fragment, the unit AI is billed by, so token share is usage share. Now the other half of the ledger: those Chinese tokens brought in under 6 percent of the money spent on the platform.

On Vercel, a major developer platform, DeepSeek went from under 1 percent of tokens to about 17 percent while bringing in about 1 percent of revenue. China is winning the traffic and losing the till.

Whether that is failure or strategy depends on your time horizon, and this is where the two races collide.

If you believe AI settles into a market like cloud computing, where a few profitable giants rent intelligence by the token, then giving it away at a loss is madness, and China's 1,100 money-losing models are a bubble deflating in slow motion.

If you believe AI settles like an operating system, where the layer everything else is built on becomes the standard and the standard-setter collects forever, then the traffic is the prize and the till fills in later.

Beijing has begun to treat the giveaway as statecraft either way. In October 2026 it circulated draft rules that would control the export of advanced AI technology itself, with thresholds based on training size and benchmark rank.

The country that built its rise on being denied technology is now drafting the paperwork to deny its own. Everybody learns the fence eventually.

I keep landing on the same thought: the giveaway is the one move in this contest that export controls cannot answer. You cannot embargo a file that has already been downloaded two billion times. America's lead is in models it sells. China's is in models the world already has.

Chapter Five

How We Got Here

None of this started with a chatbot. It started with an industrial plan, a phone company and a lesson both capitals learned from the same decade.

China announced its intentions in writing, years in advance. Made in China 2025, published in 2015, set targets for domestic content across advanced industries.

In July 2017 the New Generation AI Development Plan laid out the ladder plainly: catch up by 2020, make major breakthroughs by 2025, lead the world by 2030.

Behind the plans stood money, a state semiconductor fund that grew through three rounds to 344 billion yuan by 2024. Washington's reply arrived in stages.

ZTE was nearly put out of business by a denial order in 2018. Huawei joined the Entity List in 2019, and that same year the Netherlands quietly blocked the EUV machine Huawei's suppliers would have needed.

The full technology embargo, on chips, memory and equipment, assembled itself between 2022 and 2024. Then, in August 2023, Huawei released the Mate 60 phone with a chip made in China at a sophistication Washington believed was years away.

It was slower and costlier than the frontier. It was also proof that the fence had a ceiling.

History offers one close precedent, and both sides have read it. In the 1980s Japan's memory chip industry took the American market apart, and Washington answered with the 1986 semiconductor agreement, tariffs, and SEMATECH, a government-backed research consortium headquartered in Austin, Texas.

By 1994 American firms had retaken the lead, not by out-fencing Japan but by moving the industry up a level, from commodity memory to microprocessors and design, where the money and the leverage actually were.

The lesson cuts in two directions, and I think you have to take both. Export controls and industrial policy can work, for a while, when paired with a domestic industry that uses the time to change the game.

And the country under pressure does not simply fall behind. It adapts, concentrates, and comes back at a different point in the stack.

China under pressure went down-market, to cheap and open. Whether that was a retreat or a flanking move is the question I started with, and I still do not think it is settled.

  • 2015 to 2017

    Made in China 2025, then the AI Development Plan: parity by 2020, breakthroughs by 2025, world leadership by 2030, written down and published for anyone to read.

  • 2018 to 2019

    ZTE's denial order. Huawei lands on the Entity List. The EUV license is blocked, and ASML never ships an EUV machine to China. The lithography ceiling is set.

  • October 2022

    Washington bars A100 and H100 exports and starts the modern control regime. Tightenings follow in 2023 and 2024, reaching memory and chipmaking equipment.

  • August 2023

    The Mate 60 Pro ships with a Chinese-made near-7nm chip. Costly, slow to make, and a demonstration that the ceiling leaks.

  • January 2025

    DeepSeek R1 lands as a free download the same week Stargate, a $500 billion American build-out, is announced. The two strategies are now visible side by side: give it away, or outspend everyone.

  • 2025 to 2026

    The H20 is banned, then licensed with a revenue share. The H200 is cleared case by case in January 2026, with a cap and a 25 percent duty. Beijing bans its own champions from buying Nvidia. Six hundred thousand H200s sit in Hong Kong, approved by one capital and refused by the other.

“America owns the frontier. China owns the floor it will be installed on. The race goes to whoever fixes their own shortage first.”

My argument, in one sentence

Chapter Six · The Local Story

Houston

The abstract race has a physical address, and a surprising amount of it is here. America's bottleneck is electricity, and electricity in America increasingly means Texas.

The customer is the grid. Houston's role in the AI race is not writing models. It is supplying the power, the engineering and increasingly the generation itself, in a state whose grid now fields more data center requests than it can serve five times over. Photograph via The Savvy List.

Houston's stake in this contest is not models or chips. It is power and permission.

CenterPoint's Houston territory carries 12.2 gigawatts of firmly committed industrial load, with 8 gigawatts of data center load expected by 2029 and 3.5 gigawatts already under construction.

A gigawatt is roughly what it takes to power a mid-sized city, so read that as eight new cities' worth of demand arriving at one utility in three years.

CenterPoint raised its ten-year capital plan to $66.7 billion in July 2026, including $800 million specifically for large-load upgrades around Houston.

The city's live data center base is still modest, about 914 megawatts across 36 facilities, which is precisely why the growth numbers look the way they do: Houston is at the front of the curve, not the middle of it.

The emblematic project sits an hour southwest. Amazon's Project Eagle in Wharton County covers about 3,000 acres, carries a $10 billion price tag and 13 buildings, and promises about 300 permanent jobs.

Do the arithmetic the ribbon cuttings skip: $10 billion for 300 jobs is $33 million per job, because a data center is not a factory that employs a town. It is a power contract with a building around it.

Its groundwater permits, filed in September, cover restrooms, construction and fire protection, and Amazon says cooling will not use the water. The power supply, possibly around 780 megawatts if each building draws what similar buildings draw, remains unconfirmed.

In the new Texas economy, the scarce approvals are not land or labor. They are electrons and the right to use them.

The rest of Houston is adapting in the ways Houston does. ExxonMobil, Chevron and HPE all sit on Fortune's ranking of the fifty companies using AI most aggressively, which in practice means the energy industry is automating the business it already dominates.

Chevron signed a twenty-year deal in June 2026 to build about 2.67 gigawatts of gas-fired power for a Microsoft data center in West Texas, an oil major becoming a power utility for a software company, which tells you where the margin moved.

Port Houston adopted a formal AI policy in July. NASA's Johnson Space Center counts more than 400 AI use cases, most still pilots.

And city hall, in August, waived its own ban on incentives for power generation to hand NRG an $11 million abatement for a new peaker plant at Greens Bayou. Houston understands, in its bones, that it sells energy.

AI is simply the newest customer, and by far the hungriest.

The build-out, from the air

474 GW asked.

Nine and a half approved. The queue is not a plan, it is a wish list, and the grid underneath it already peaked at 91 gigawatts. Photograph via Stardog.

Chapter Seven

Texas

Texas is where the American bottleneck gets governed, or not. The state holds roughly a third of the country's planned capacity and a new governor who campaigned against how it got there.

Start with what Texas already is. Dallas ranks as the number one primary data center market in the world.

The state counts over 400 operating facilities, about 12 gigawatts under construction as of October 2026, and roughly 30 percent of all American data center capacity scheduled to come online in 2028.

Stargate's Abilene campus, the flagship of the $500 billion announcement, had 618 megawatts delivered across six of eight buildings by September, with a Microsoft campus next door taking the full site to 2.1 gigawatts.

Abilene also shows the local bill: an 85 percent property tax abatement, rents up about 50 percent in a year, sales tax revenue up $17 million, and fatal crashes in Taylor County up about 30 percent on construction traffic.

The boom is real, and so is everything attached to it.

The state's rulebook is being rewritten in real time, and the dates matter more than the speeches.

SB 6, signed in June 2025, put the biggest loads under new discipline: study fees, backup generation requirements, and curtailment obligations, meaning a data center can be ordered to cut its draw when the grid is stressed.

A Public Utility Commission rule effective October 2026 requires security of $50,000 per megawatt from large loads, real money posted against real commitments, which is one way to separate builders from speculators in that 474 gigawatt queue.

The commission's cost allocation rewrite, due December 31, 2026, decides the question underneath every Texas rate case: whether the $33 billion transmission backbone being built for this load gets paid for by the data centers that caused it, or spread across every household bill in the state, where transmission already runs 12 to 20 percent of a typical residential charge.

Meanwhile the state's data center sales tax exemption, worth $5.4 million in 2014, will cost an estimated $1.6 billion in fiscal 2027 and about $9 billion cumulatively through 2030.

Legislators of both parties sat through a nine-hour hearing in August and came out talking about repeal.

Then Texas changed governors. On November 3, 2026, Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott, 52.8 percent to 45.7 percent, becoming the first Democratic governor since Ann Richards and the first Latina governor in state history.

She campaigned on an immediate moratorium on new data center approvals, an end to subsidies and nondisclosure agreements, and a community say in siting. As of November 9, no draft moratorium text exists.

Jefferies counts 13.3 gigawatts of announced Texas projects at immediate risk if one arrives.

The constraints on her are as real as her mandate: the Senate stayed Republican, 19 to 12, the environmental commission that issues permits is staffed by Abbott appointees with terms running to 2027 and 2031, and the projects already approved are already financed.

A governor can slow the queue. She cannot unbuild Abilene.

I read Texas as the American bottleneck in miniature, which makes it, in my view, the most important AI jurisdiction in the country that never appears in the benchmark stories. China's constraint is a machine it cannot buy.

America's constraint is a set of decisions it has not made: who pays for transmission, who gets curtailed, whose water, whose tax break.

Those decisions now run through Austin, on deadlines printed in this section, and they will move the frontier gap more than the next model release will.

Chapter Eight

What Comes Next

Two honest ways to read everything above. They disagree about which race matters, and each one names the evidence that would prove it.

Read A

The split persists

America keeps the frontier because compute, capital and, barely, power hold together. China keeps the cheap layer and slowly turns distribution into standards, the way a free operating system becomes the default everything is built on.

Ten years from now there are two AI worlds, interoperable at the edges, each dominant at home and in its sphere, and the question of who won stops making sense.

Decide by: H200 licensing stays narrow. American grid connections keep clearing. Anthropic and OpenAI revenue keeps compounding faster than their commitments come due.

Read B

The cheap layer eats the frontier

Most real work never needed the smartest model, only a good one at a tenth of the price. Efficiency, distribution and a Chinese inference chip that is merely adequate compress the frontier premium until the expensive race stops paying for itself.

The contest is decided by who ships, not who benchmarks, and it is decided sooner than the frontier labs expect.

Decide by: a Chinese memory or inference breakthrough. An American power moratorium or a credit event in the AI financing circle. China's 1,100 labs consolidating into one or two winners with real revenue.

What would change my mind is concrete, and it is the same list either way. If China's accessible compute doubles again by the end of 2027 while its memory yields stay under 30 percent, Read A is winning on points.

If CXMT's yields cross 50 percent, or a Hinojosa moratorium survives the Legislature and starts cancelling financed projects, the bottleneck race has a new leader.

Until one of those things happens, the scoreboard reads the way the headline says: two races, two leaders, no champion.

Chapter Nine

Watchlist

Five dates that move this story. Put them on the calendar.

  • 1December 10, 2026: the ERCOT reports Batch Zero gets its verdicts. Which of the 362 conditionally included projects are real, and which were queue positions held for resale, becomes public information.
  • 2December 31, 2026: the PUCT cost rule Who pays for $33 billion of Texas transmission, data centers or households, is decided in a rule most Texans will never read and every Texan will pay for.
  • 3January 2027: the Hong Kong chips H200 license decisions land and 600,000 stockpiled processors either move or rot. Movement means the fence is now a tariff. Rot means Beijing's refusal is permanent policy.
  • 4January 19, 2027: inauguration in Austin Governor Hinojosa takes office. A published moratorium draft, or the absence of one, tells you whether the campaign promise was a policy or a slogan. Jefferies counts 13.3 gigawatts riding on the answer.
  • 5Fourth-quarter earnings, early 2027 Anthropic and OpenAI report run rates against $895 billion and roughly $720 billion of commitments. Revenue catching the promises is the whole ballgame for Read A.

That is where I land. Two countries set out to win the same race and ended up running different ones, each convinced the other's event is the preliminary.

The frontier is American, expensive and financed. The floor is Chinese, cheap and already installed in more places every week.

Somewhere between a Hong Kong warehouse full of unwanted chips and a Texas queue five times the size of the grid, the actual future of this technology is being decided, in gigawatts and yields and license clauses, by people whose names never appear in the benchmark headlines.

Watch the bottlenecks. They are the scoreboard that does not lie.
